title: Why you should write tests first - Uncle Bob
summary: Short clip arguing that writing tests after the fact leaves holes in the suite, while test-first forces decoupled design and produces a suite you can trust.

assertions.quote: you walk away and you leave a hole in the test Suite

verdicts.note: The mechanism is plausible and matches practitioner experience, but controlled TDD studies measure defects and productivity rather than coverage gaps, so the size of the effect is not established.

Test-last developers wrote as many unit-test asserts as TDD developers (sign test p=1.00, Cliff's delta 0.07), though in a 3-hour kata with incremental test-last there is little hard-to-test code to skip.

The review grants that TDD yields more tests than test-last, but reports that test quality, maintainability and co-evolution with production code get little attention, so more tests is not the same as fewer holes.

In every study but one, test-first programmers' tests covered a higher share of code, and several student test-last teams wrote no automated tests, reporting they ran out of time; the study shows the lower coverage but not that hard-to-test code was what got skipped.

Method, statement and branch coverage were all significantly higher in the TDD project even though every team was encouraged to write tests, and the test-last teams' tests were less thorough; why the gaps arose is not analysed.

assertions.quote: you cannot write the code that's hard to test if you write the test first

verdicts.note: Studies of TDD find modest improvements in some internal quality metrics such as coupling and cohesion, with mixed results overall and effects that depend on developer experience.

Across three industry quasi-experiments, an industry case study and two student experiments, test-first code came in more and smaller, less complex and more highly tested units, but the authors could not confirm that TDD lowers coupling or improves cohesion (CBO and fan-out differences small and not significant, parameter counts higher test-first).

In three nine-week student projects (one TDD, two iterative test-last), TDD code was only slightly less coupled with differences too small to conclude anything, and was significantly less cohesive, so TDD did not automatically produce the better design claimed, though its test coverage was much higher.

assertions.quote: a test Suite that does does not allow you to make a decision when it passes is a useless test Suite

verdicts.note: A framing about what trust in a suite means rather than a measurable outcome; partial suites still catch some regressions.
Controlled studies show TDD lowers defect density at some cost in development time; direct measurements of debugging time are scarce.

assertions.quote: every time you make a test pass there's a little shot of endorphins to the back of your brain

verdicts.note: A claim about enjoyment and motivation that varies by person.

assertions.quote: the most profound effect is that button and the fact that you trust it

verdicts.note: Survey research such as DORA links reliable test automation with higher delivery confidence and performance, but the direction of causation is not isolated.

DORA 2019 finds automated testing predicts continuous integration, which predicts continuous delivery, and frames the mechanism as developers trusting that a passing suite means deployable code; the fear/confidence effect itself is asserted, not measured, and the data are survey self-reports.
